patterns_detected.description: Queries joining 3+ tables with multiple join conditions. Aurora's query optimizer excels at complex join planning: hash joins, merge joins, and nested loop selection are automatic and performant at scale.
Aggregation queries with GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG). Aurora handles analytical aggregations efficiently with parallel query execution.

Multi-table write operations within transaction context with FK constraints. Aurora provides full ACID compliance with multi-statement transactions; NoSQL engines cannot replicate this without application-level coordination.

Tables with high foreign key density (>2 FKs) and CASCADE operations. Relational engines enforce referential integrity at the database level; migrating to NoSQL would require application-level enforcement.

Reporting queries with large result sets, date-range filters, and ordered/limited aggregate results. Aurora's read replicas can offload reporting workloads without impacting transactional performance.
Correlated subqueries using EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, or IN (SELECT ...). Aurora's optimizer can decorrelate and flatten these into efficient join plans.
UPDATE or DELETE operations with complex WHERE clauses affecting multiple rows. Aurora handles bulk mutations with row-level locking and MVCC, maintaining consistency without full-table locks.

Pagination patterns using OFFSET/LIMIT or cursor-based keyset pagination (WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT N). Aurora handles pagination efficiently with index-based seeks; NoSQL engines handle pagination poorly.
Queries joining 2 tables. While simpler than multi-table complex joins, these still require a relational engine with a query optimizer; NoSQL engines cannot perform server-side joins.

Standard single-table CRUD operations (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) at moderate frequency. These are valid relational workloads; Aurora handles them efficiently with connection pooling and buffer cache.

Batch lookups using WHERE column IN (...) with multiple values: one index scan probes every listed value (PostgreSQL documentation, Indexes, a ScalarArrayOpExpr on a B-tree; MySQL Reference Manual, Range Optimization, equality ranges for IN lists), with no item limit, where DynamoDB's BatchGetItem takes at most 100 keys and 16 MB (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, BatchGetItem). In the key-lookup class it raises no score: key-value-lookup rates the same read at 80.

A read of one row, or an IN-list batch, by its full primary or unique key: a B-tree index point read, served from memory once cached, with read replicas to scale the reads (PostgreSQL documentation, Index Types; MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes).

Recursive CTEs (WITH RECURSIVE) for hierarchical data traversal: org charts, category trees, bills of materials, with the SEARCH and CYCLE clauses for traversal order and cycle detection and no default recursion limit (PostgreSQL documentation, WITH Queries).

Window functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD) for running totals, rankings and row-level analytics, in one pass without self-joins, with the ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS frame modes and frame exclusion (PostgreSQL documentation, Window Function Calls).

JSONB operations (->>, @>, jsonb_agg, jsonb_build_object) for semi-structured data within relational context. Aurora PG provides GIN-indexed JSONB queries, combining document flexibility with relational joins.
Array operations (ANY, array_agg, unnest) for multi-value attributes. Aurora PG handles array containment queries with GIN indexes, avoiding junction tables for simple multi-value cases.
Native full-text search using to_tsvector, ts_query, and @@ operator. Aurora PG provides built-in full-text with GIN indexes, suitable for moderate search workloads without a separate search engine.
UPSERT with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and RETURNING clause. Aurora PG handles atomic insert-or-update in a single statement with row-level locking, with no read-modify-write cycle needed.

A write whose rows come from a join with another table (UPDATE ... FROM, DELETE ... USING), run set-based in one statement; an UPDATE or DELETE changes its one target table, and changing several tables in one statement takes a chain of data-modifying WITH queries where MySQL's multiple-table UPDATE needs none (PostgreSQL documentation, UPDATE; WITH Queries, Data-Modifying Statements in WITH).

anti_patterns_detected.description: Table with no foreign keys and no join participation: all queries are single-table CRUD. Aurora serves single-table CRUD natively and uses none of its relational features for it (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora). This workload has no structural relational requirement and could run on a simpler, purpose-built engine (DynamoDB for key-value, ElastiCache for hot lookups).
anti_patterns_detected.recommendation: Evaluate whether this table benefits from Aurora's relational features. If it's purely key-value access, DynamoDB offers better cost/performance. If it's a hot lookup, ElastiCache is more appropriate.

anti_patterns_detected.description: Table accessed by at most 2 distinct query patterns, all single-table, all by primary key or single column filter. Aurora serves these reads natively and its query optimizer adds nothing to them (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora). This is a key-value workload wearing a relational costume, with no query optimizer benefit.
anti_patterns_detected.recommendation: Consider DynamoDB for simple key-value access or ElastiCache for sub-millisecond lookups. Aurora adds connection overhead and query parsing cost for access patterns that don't need them.
